patients.summary: Retired man who joined in 2019 with diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, a treated prostate cancer and a remote stroke. His PSA recurs in 2021 (salvage radiation, then surveillance), nephrogenic diabetes insipidus follows in 2022, and cognitive decline to vascular dementia by 2024; after his last visit in September 2024 the practice receives records of a stroke admission and an ED visit for ventricular tachycardia.

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
NEW PATIENT VISIT

69 y/o retired man moving his care here from a practice he left after his doctor retired. Wants one place that keeps track of everything.

HPI / PROBLEMS HE BRINGS
1. Type 2 diabetes x about 10 yrs. Metformin 1000 twice a day, no lows, does not check sugars at home much. Last A1c he remembers was 'around 7.'
2. Hypertension x about 15 yrs. Lisinopril 20 daily. Home cuff 'usually 130s.'
3. High cholesterol, atorvastatin 40, no muscle aches.
4. Prostate cancer, radical prostatectomy spring 2018. Says his PSA has been 'zero' at every check since. Recovered well from the surgery.
5. Stroke 2016 - in the hospital a few days, fully recovered. No residual weakness or speech problem.

MEDS: metformin 1000 mg BID, lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily.
ALLERGIES: none known.
PSH: radical prostatectomy 2018.
FH: father had prostate cancer (diagnosed in his 70s), mother had a stroke, sister has type 2 diabetes.
SH: retired. Never smoked. Doesn't drink. Lives in Belchertown. Daughter lives nearby. Drives.

ROS: no chest pain, no dyspnea, no urinary trouble, no numbness in feet, no vision change.

EXAM: BP 138/86. Wt 89 kg, ht 175 cm, BMI 29. Pleasant, clear historian.
HEENT normal. Neck supple, no bruit. Heart RRR, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abd soft, well-healed lower midline scar. No edema. Feet: skin intact, monofilament normal both feet, DP pulses 2+. Neuro: strength and speech normal, gait steady.

A/P
- T2DM: continue metformin. A1c, CMP, ACR today.
- HTN: a little above goal today, continue lisinopril, bring home readings next time.
- HLD: lipid panel.
- Prostate cancer s/p RP: PSA today; he was followed by his surgeon's office, records requested.
- Hx stroke: no residual deficit; records requested from prior practice.
- HM: hep C screen today (one-time). Flu shot next month at nurse visit. Wellness visit in December.

RTC 3 months.

documents.title: Records Request

documents.body: Signed release from pt. Records request faxed to his previous primary care office and to the urology office that did his surgery. Asked for last 5 yrs of notes, labs, op report, PSA history, imaging, immunizations.

documents.title: Your Lab Results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Hi Mr. Pickett,

Your first set of labs is back. Your A1c is right about where we want it for you. Kidney function and potassium are fine, and so is your cholesterol on the atorvastatin. PSA is undetectable, which is what we hope to see after your surgery. Hepatitis C screen is negative, and your urine protein check is normal.

No changes. See you for the flu shot and then in December.

Your primary care physician

documents.title: Prior Practice and Urology Records
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Outside records received from his prior primary care office and urology, about 60 pages. Reviewed.

Highlights:
- Radical prostatectomy, spring 2018. Postop PSAs listed as undetectable (<0.1) at each check through spring 2019. Urology planned PSA every 6 months, then yearly; can be done here.
- 2016 hospital summary: admitted for an ischemic stroke; symptoms cleared before discharge. No residual deficit at the follow-up note.
- Colonoscopy 2015: normal, no polyps. No repeat recommended given age at next interval.
- Tdap 2017. Pneumococcal and zoster: none documented.
- A1c values 6.8-7.3 over the past several years on metformin. LDLs 80s-90s on atorvastatin 40.

Problem list and medication list here match. Scanned to chart.

documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
BP recheck as planned.

He has cut back salt, home log is mostly 140s over upper 80s. Office 146/88 after sitting. Pulse in the 80s. No headaches, chest pain, dizziness.

Exam: heart regular, no murmur; lungs clear; no edema.

A/P
HTN above goal in a man with a prior ischemic stroke and diabetes. Talked over options. Adding metoprolol succinate 25 mg daily on top of lisinopril, to bring the pressure down and for his overall cardiovascular risk. Reviewed side effects (tiredness, slow pulse, lightheadedness). BMP today. Follow up in about 3 months with fasting labs (A1c, lipids, BMP) and a PSA, which is due.

documents.title: Question about new pill
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Doctor, does the metoprolol need to go with the others in the morning or can I take it at night? I keep forgetting which one it is. Thanks, Bernie

documents.title: RE: Question about new pill
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Hi Bernie, morning with your other pills is fine, and keeping them all together is the easiest way not to miss it. It's the small white tablet. A pillbox can help. Call if you feel dizzy when you stand up.

documents.title: Oncology Consultation
documents.author: oncology
documents.body:
OUTPATIENT ONCOLOGY - NEW CONSULTATION
Date of service: 08/02/2021
Referred by: primary care, for rising PSA

Patient is a 71-year-old man treated with radical prostatectomy three years ago, recovery uncomplicated. PSA stayed undetectable afterward; on 2/2/2021 it was <0.1. Since then it has climbed, 2.2 in May and 4.5 today. Over roughly six months he has felt progressively more fatigued and has had hesitancy starting his stream. He reports no bone pain and no weight loss, fevers or sweats.

PMH: type 2 diabetes, hypertension (both well controlled per pt and PCP records), hyperlipidemia, prostate cancer s/p RP 2018, ischemic stroke 2016 without residual deficit.
Meds: metformin 1000 mg BID, lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, metoprolol succinate 25 mg daily.
Allergies: NKDA.
FH: father with prostate cancer; mother stroke; sister type 2 DM.
SH: retired, never smoker, no alcohol. Daughter accompanies.

Exam: Well appearing. No spinal or bony tenderness. DRE: no abnormality appreciated. No lymphadenopathy. No edema.

Labs today: Hgb 13.2, creatinine 1.1, fasting glucose 142, total cholesterol 178. PSA 4.5 ng/mL.
Whole-body bone scan (7/28/2021): no scintigraphic evidence of osseous metastatic disease.

Impression: Biochemically recurrent prostate adenocarcinoma after radical prostatectomy, PSA 4.5, no metastatic disease on bone scan.

Plan:
- Refer to radiation oncology to discuss salvage radiation to the prostate bed.
- Urology to follow urinary symptoms and PSA after treatment.
- Copy to PCP.

Oncology

documents.title: Oncology Letter Review
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Oncology letter received and reviewed with pt and daughter by phone. Bone scan negative. Plan is radiation to the area where the prostate was; radiation oncology will call. Answered questions about whether he needs to stop any of his medicines for it - no. Will see him in the fall once treatment is done.

documents.title: Radiation Oncology Consultation
documents.author: radiation oncology
documents.body:
RADIATION ONCOLOGY CONSULTATION
Date of service: 8/23/2021

71 y/o man, prostatectomy 2018, PSA now 4.5 and rising from undetectable in early 2021. Bone scan negative. Seen with his daughter.

We discussed salvage external beam radiation to the prostate bed, the expected course (about 7 weeks, weekdays), and short- and long-term effects including urinary frequency and urgency, bowel irritation, fatigue, and later bladder or ureter changes. Hormonal therapy alongside radiation was discussed; with his stroke history and cardiovascular risk, he and the team agreed to radiation alone.

Allergies: NKDA. Meds per PCP list.

Plan: CT simulation next week, start early September. 66 Gy in 33 fractions.

Radiation Oncology

documents.title: Radiation Treatment Summary
documents.author: radiation oncology
documents.body:
RADIATION THERAPY COMPLETION SUMMARY

Diagnosis: biochemically recurrent prostate adenocarcinoma after radical prostatectomy.
Treatment: external beam radiation to the prostate bed, 66 Gy in 33 fractions, 9/7/2021 through 10/26/2021. No breaks. No androgen deprivation.

Tolerance: urinary frequency in the second half of treatment, mild fatigue. No bowel bleeding. No unplanned visits.

Follow-up: PSA in about 3 months with urology. Late effects reviewed again with patient and daughter.

Allergies: NKDA.

Radiation Oncology

UROLOGY CLINIC NOTE
Date of visit: 2/14/2022

Returning to our clinic, where he had his prostatectomy in 2018, after oncology evaluation and salvage radiation to the prostate bed (completed 10/2021).

He describes six months of getting up at night to void, hesitancy, and a weaker stream. No dysuria and no burning.

PMH: hypertension, type 2 diabetes on metformin, hyperlipidemia, ischemic stroke 2016.
Meds: metformin 1000 mg BID, lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, metoprolol succinate 25 mg daily.
Allergies: NKDA.
FH: father diagnosed with prostate cancer at 75.
SH: nonsmoker, no alcohol.

Exam: BP 135/85, HR 78, BMI 29. Abdomen soft. DRE: smooth prostatic fossa, no palpable mass or nodularity, nontender.

Labs: PSA 6.5 ng/mL. BMP and UA unremarkable.

Assessment: Prostate cancer with persistent PSA rise after salvage radiation. Lower urinary tract symptoms after prostatectomy and pelvic radiation.

Plan:
- We discussed androgen deprivation. Given his strokes and cardiovascular risk, and the PSA pace so far, we will hold off and follow PSA every 6 months (PCP can draw).
- Timed voiding, limit evening fluids.
- Return in one year, sooner if bone pain or rapid PSA rise.

Urology

documents.title: Office Visit - Nocturia
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
CC: getting up all night to urinate.

HPI: Over the last couple of months the nighttime trips have gotten worse, now several a night, and he says it is a lot of urine each time, pale like water. He has stopped drinking anything after supper and it hasn't helped. Not especially thirsty during the day, he thinks. Tired from broken sleep. No burning, no blood, no flank pain, no fever.

Meds: metformin, lisinopril, atorvastatin, metoprolol succinate. No diuretic.

O: Vitals per flowsheet. Well appearing, mucous membranes moist. Abd soft, no suprapubic fullness or tenderness. No edema.

A/P
Nocturnal polyuria, large dilute volumes, not just the bladder-outlet pattern urology described. Glucose has been fine so this isn't sugar. Checking BMP (Na, Ca, glucose), urine osm, UA, A1c.
If urine is dilute with a normal-to-high sodium, will send to nephrology for a diabetes insipidus workup.

documents.title: Result Note
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Na 143, glucose and calcium normal. Urine osm 190, SG 1.004 - dilute urine. UA otherwise negative. Nephrology referral placed.

documents.title: Test results and kidney referral
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Hi Bernie,

Your sugar and blood salts are normal, but your urine is very watery even after you cut back on fluids. That can happen when the kidneys don't respond to the hormone that normally concentrates urine. I've asked a kidney specialist to see you to test for that. Their office will call. Keep drinking when you're thirsty during the day - don't hold back because of the bathroom trips.

Your primary care physician

documents.title: RE: Test results and kidney referral
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Thank you. My daughter Ellen will drive me, can you put her name down so they can talk to her too. - B. Pickett

reports.text:
RENAL ULTRASOUND
Indication: nocturnal polyuria; prior prostatectomy and pelvic radiation.
Right kidney 10.8 cm, left kidney 11.1 cm, normal cortical thickness and echogenicity. No renal stones. No renal mass. Both ureters are dilated along their visualized course. No ureteral stone or obstructing mass identified. Bladder adequately distended, wall smooth, no intraluminal mass.
reports.conclusion: Bilateral hydroureters without stones or obstructing masses.

documents.title: Nephrology Consultation
documents.author: nephrology
documents.body:
NEPHROLOGY CONSULTATION
Date of service: 08/09/2022
Reason: nocturnal polyuria with dilute urine (urine osm 190, SG 1.004 per PCP)

HPI: 72-year-old man with prostate cancer treated by radical prostatectomy and then salvage radiation to the prostate bed roughly a year ago. Urology saw him in February for hesitancy and nocturia. Over the last four months the night voiding has steadily worsened: he gets up repeatedly and passes large volumes of clear urine though he stops fluids well before bed. Some daytime sleepiness from the interrupted nights. No dysuria, no visible blood, no flank pain. No fever, weight loss or abdominal pain.

Meds: metformin 1000 mg BID, lisinopril 20 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, metoprolol succinate 25 mg.
Allergies: NKDA.
FH: father prostate cancer, mother stroke, sister T2DM.
SH: never smoker, no alcohol, retired.

Exam: vitals within normal limits. Abdomen soft, no masses felt, no suprapubic tenderness.

Data: serum glucose, calcium and electrolytes normal today. Renal ultrasound today: bilateral hydroureters, no stones or obstructing mass.
Desmopressin challenge in clinic: urine osmolality rose by less than 10 percent.

Assessment: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (no response to desmopressin with dilute urine and normal serum chemistries). Bilateral hydroureters after prostatectomy and pelvic radiation, no obstructing lesion seen.

Plan:
- Start hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg daily plus a low-sodium diet (handout given) to reduce urine volume.
- Drink to thirst.
- BMP in about a month (PCP fine) for sodium and potassium.
- Repeat renal ultrasound in 6 months.

Nephrology

documents.body: Daughter Ellen (on HIPAA form) called ahead of Monday's visit. Over the past year he's been forgetting conversations they had a day or two before, and he's been mixing up his bills - two late notices and one paid twice. Says he always handled money carefully. No falls, no sudden changes, no new weakness that she has seen. She wanted the doctor to know before the visit since he tends to say everything is fine. Message to PCP.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Office Visit - Memory
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Visit with daughter, who called last week (see RN note).

S: Pt himself thinks his memory is 'a little worse, like anybody my age.' Daughter describes a year of forgetting recent conversations and errors with bills that are new for him. No getting lost driving per daughter. Mood ok, sleeping better since the HCTZ. PHQ-9 3.
Meds unchanged.

O: Vitals per flowsheet. Pleasant, conversant, repeats one question during the visit. Speech fluent. Strength symmetric, gait steady. Heart regular, lungs clear.

A/P
Progressive memory complaint over a year with functional change (finances), in a man with a prior ischemic stroke, diabetes and hypertension. Needs formal cognitive evaluation.
- Neurology referral.
- BMP (sodium on HCTZ, calcium) and CBC today; neurology can add the rest.
- Daughter to help with bills in the meantime; she's already set up autopay.
- Continue meds.

RTC after neurology, ~Sept for wellness visit.

documents.title: Neurology Consultation
documents.author: neurology
documents.body:
NEUROLOGY - COGNITIVE EVALUATION
Date of visit: 8/7/2023
Referring: primary care

History obtained from patient and his daughter, who helps care for him. He had an ischemic stroke in 2016 without lasting deficit. Over the past year the family has noticed he loses track of recent conversations and has started making mistakes with his finances, which he always managed without trouble. He feels his memory is only mildly off.

PMH: T2DM, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, prostate cancer s/p RP and salvage RT with PSA surveillance, nephrogenic DI.
Meds: metformin 1000 BID, lisinopril 20, atorvastatin 40, metoprolol succinate 25, hydrochlorothiazide 12.5.
Allergies: NKDA.
FH: father prostate cancer, mother stroke, sister T2DM.
SH: retired, never smoker, no alcohol.

Exam: Awake, cooperative. Knows who he is and where he is; gives the wrong month and year. Struggles to come up with his grandchildren's names and cannot describe what he did yesterday. MMSE 22/30. Cranial nerves, strength, reflexes, sensation, coordination and gait otherwise normal.

Labs: fasting glucose 130, A1c 7.2, total cholesterol 190, LDL 100, HDL 45, triglycerides 250, TSH 2.5, B12 400.

Impression: Mild cognitive impairment, likely vascular in a man with prior stroke and vascular risk factors. Reversible contributors not found on thyroid and B12 testing.

Plan:
- Continue vascular risk-factor management with PCP.
- Daughter to supervise finances and medications.
- Repeat assessment in one year, sooner with any sudden change.

Neurology

documents.title: Annual Wellness Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
MEDICARE AWV, SUBSEQUENT. Daughter present.

Neurology letter 8/7 reviewed: MMSE 22, mild cognitive impairment of likely vascular origin; TSH and B12 normal.

Function: independent in dressing, bathing, eating, walking. Daughter now handles bills and fills his weekly pillbox. He still cooks simple meals. No falls this year. PHQ-2 0.

Advance care planning (separate, about 20 min): daughter remains health care proxy, form on file updated. He would want treatment for anything reversible; he does not want to end up on machines long term. MOLST not completed today; he wants to think about it.

Prevention: colonoscopy aged out. Flu, updated COVID and RSV next month at nurse visit. Shingrix and PCV20 done.

Chronic: DM2, HTN, HLD, nephrogenic DI on HCTZ, prostate cancer on PSA surveillance (PSA today for urology), MCI.

Plan: labs as ordered. Diabetes recheck in December.

events.reason: Cognitive decline, transient spells; ordered by neurology

reports.text:
MRI BRAIN WITHOUT CONTRAST
Indication: progressive cognitive decline, transient episodes of confusion and weakness.
Technique: multiplanar multisequence MRI of the brain without contrast.
Findings: Multiple small infarcts in the left cerebral hemisphere. Extensive periventricular white matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensity. No restricted diffusion. No hemorrhage. No mass or extra-axial collection. Ventricles and sulci appropriate for age. Major intracranial flow voids preserved.
reports.conclusion: Multiple small infarcts in the left cerebral hemisphere and extensive periventricular white matter changes. No acute infarct, hemorrhage or mass.

documents.title: MRI Brain
documents.author: radiology
documents.body: Outside MRI brain without contrast, 8/5/2024, ordered by neurology. Report received and scanned. Impression: multiple small infarcts in the left cerebral hemisphere and extensive periventricular white matter changes; nothing acute.

documents.title: Neurology Follow-up
documents.author: neurology
documents.body:
NEUROLOGY FOLLOW-UP
Date: 8/12/2024

Returns one year after evaluation for cognitive decline, with his daughter. She describes a slow loss over the past year of his ability to plan and organize, for example he can no longer put together a grocery list or keep track of a week's plans. In the last six months there were two spells of abrupt confusion with weakness, each lasting several hours and then clearing; the family did not seek care at the time. He acknowledges some forgetfulness; what bothers him most is no longer being able to handle his money.

Meds: metformin 1000 BID, lisinopril 20, atorvastatin 40, metoprolol succinate 25, HCTZ 12.5.
Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: BP 145/90. Mild weakness of the right arm and leg. Deep tendon reflexes brisker on the right. Remainder of exam as before.

Labs: A1c 7.8, fasting glucose 162, total cholesterol 190, LDL 110, HDL 45.
MRI brain 8/5/2024: multiple small left hemispheric infarcts and extensive periventricular white matter disease.

Impression: Vascular dementia. Progression from last year's mild cognitive impairment with loss of independent function, new focal right-sided signs and imaging showing multiple infarcts on a background of small vessel disease.

Plan:
- Blood pressure, diabetes and lipid management with PCP.
- Daughter to continue managing finances and medications; home safety reviewed.
- Return in one year, sooner for any new sudden symptoms (call 911).

Neurology

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Follow-up after neurology, with daughter.

Neurology 8/12 reviewed: now vascular dementia; two transient spells of confusion/weakness this year that were not evaluated at the time; mild R-sided weakness, brisk R reflexes; MRI multiple small L hemisphere infarcts + extensive white matter disease. A1c 7.8, LDL 110 on their labs.

S: He says he feels fine. Daughter: no further spells since spring. She manages the pillbox and bills; he still lives on his own with her checking daily. No falls. Voiding stable.

O: BP 144/88, rechecked similar. Pulse 70s. Alert, a bit slowed in conversation. Mild R-sided weakness as neurology found. Gait slow but steady. Heart regular, lungs clear, no edema. Feet ok.

A/P
1. Vascular dementia - per neurology. Daughter knows to call 911 for any sudden symptoms.
2. HTN - above goal today. Daughter will check home BP twice a week for a month and send the log; we'll decide then.
3. DM2 - A1c 7.8 on metformin. Diet review; recheck in 3 months.
4. HLD - on atorvastatin 40.
5. Nephrogenic DI - BMP today.
6. Prostate ca - PSA today for urology.
7. ACR today.

No medication changes today. RTC 3 months - daughter will schedule.

Hi Ellen and Bernie,

Kidney function, potassium and sodium are all fine on the water pill. Urine protein check is normal. PSA is 9.1, up a little from 8.7 in February - I've sent it to urology, and it's in keeping with the slow rise they've been watching.

Please send the home blood pressure readings in a few weeks, and book the December visit when you get a chance.

Your primary care physician

Please call the front desk for the first opening that works - we can do an early morning slot. He's also due for his flu and COVID shots; the pharmacy can give those if the office is hard to get to.

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: hospitalist
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY - regional hospital, inpatient medicine
Admitted 4/28/2025, discharged 5/1/2025

Discharge diagnosis: acute ischemic stroke.
Other: vascular dementia, T2DM, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, prostate cancer on surveillance, nephrogenic DI.

Brought in by daughter for worse walking and right-sided weakness compared with his baseline. CT head on arrival: multiple areas of infarction in both cerebral hemispheres, no hemorrhage.

Course: admitted for monitoring and therapy evaluation. Able to walk with assistance by discharge. Evaluated by PT and OT; discharged home with daughter's support and home physical therapy.

Discharge medications (unchanged from home): metformin 1000 mg BID, lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, metoprolol succinate 25 mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg daily.
Allergies: NKDA.

Follow-up: PCP within 1-2 weeks; neurology as scheduled.

Hospitalist

Offered a post-hospital visit this week or next with PCP; daughter said he's worn out from the hospital and she'd rather wait, will call when he's up to it. Reviewed stroke warning signs and 911. Message to PCP.

events.reason: Vascular dementia follow-up after stroke admission

documents.title: Neurology Follow-up
documents.author: neurology
documents.body:
NEUROLOGY FOLLOW-UP
Date: 7/29/2025

Vascular dementia, seen with his daughter, three months after a hospital stay for ischemic stroke. Since that admission she has seen an abrupt drop in what he can do day to day; he can no longer manage any part of his money and needs prompting for ordinary tasks. He is also more irritable, and walking has been harder since the stroke.

Meds: metformin 1000 BID, lisinopril 20, atorvastatin 40, metoprolol succinate 25, HCTZ 12.5.
Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: Mild right hemiparesis. Romberg positive. Gait slow and unsteady. MMSE 24/30, points lost mainly on attention and calculation.
Imaging: admission CT head (4/28/2025) reviewed - multiple infarcts in both cerebral hemispheres.

Impression: Vascular dementia with stepwise decline after the recent stroke; gait impairment.

Plan:
- Outpatient physical therapy for gait and balance.
- Home safety: grab bars, remove loose rugs, supervision on stairs.
- Risk-factor management with PCP.
- Return in 6 months.

Neurology

reports.text:
12-LEAD ECG
Rate 150. Regular wide-complex tachycardia. AV dissociation present. QRS axis and morphology consistent with ventricular origin.
Repeat after amiodarone (14:58): sinus rhythm, rate 72, normal intervals, no acute ST changes.
reports.conclusion: Ventricular tachycardia at 150 with AV dissociation; converted to sinus rhythm.

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT RECORD - regional hospital
Date of visit: 1/28/2026

CC: palpitations, lightheaded.

HPI: 75-year-old man with vascular dementia and prior strokes, brought by daughter. About 30 minutes before arrival, while repotting houseplants at the kitchen table, he suddenly felt his heart racing and became lightheaded. No chest pain, no shortness of breath, did not pass out.

PMH: vascular dementia, ischemic strokes, T2DM, HTN, HLD, prostate cancer on surveillance, nephrogenic DI.
Meds: metformin, lisinopril, atorvastatin, metoprolol succinate 25 mg, HCTZ.
Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: BP 110/70, HR 150, RR 18. Alert and oriented. Heart rhythm regular, no murmurs, rubs or gallops. Lungs clear bilaterally. Neck veins: intermittent prominent jugular venous pulsations, not matching the heartbeat.

ECG obtained immediately: regular wide-complex tachycardia at 150 with AV dissociation - ventricular tachycardia.

ED course: hemodynamically stable. Amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 minutes; converted to sinus rhythm at 72. Labs: potassium 4.3, magnesium 2.1, high-sensitivity troponin I 9 ng/L, creatinine 1.2.

Assessment: Sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, hemodynamically tolerated, converted with amiodarone.
Disposition: admitted to telemetry under cardiology.

Emergency Medicine

reports.text:
TRANSTHORACIC ECHOCARDIOGRAM
Indication: ventricular tachycardia.
Left ventricle normal in size and wall thickness. LVEF 55-60%. Normal regional wall motion. Right ventricle normal size and function. Atria normal in size. No significant valvular stenosis or regurgitation. No pericardial effusion. IVC normal with respiratory variation.
reports.conclusion: Normal LV size and function, LVEF 55-60%, normal wall motion, no significant valve disease.

documents.title: Cardiology Discharge Summary
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY - cardiology service
Admitted 1/28/2026 via ED, discharged 1/30/2026

Principal diagnosis: sustained ventricular tachycardia, converted with IV amiodarone in the ED.

Course: Two nights on telemetry with no recurrence of VT. Electrolytes normal. Echocardiogram: LVEF 55-60%, normal wall motion, no significant valve disease. Metoprolol succinate increased from 25 mg to 50 mg daily. Outpatient ischemic evaluation and rhythm monitoring arranged with cardiology clinic.

Discharge medications: metformin 1000 mg BID, lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily (increased), hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg daily.
Allergies: NKDA.

Follow-up: cardiology clinic in 4-6 weeks; PCP.

Cardiology

documents.title: Urology Follow-up
documents.author: urology
documents.body:
UROLOGY FOLLOW-UP
2/23/2026

Prostate cancer, RP 2018 and salvage RT 2021, PSA surveillance. With daughter. Hospital stay last month for a heart rhythm problem, now on a higher metoprolol dose.
PSA 9.8 (2/25) -> 10.6 today. No bone pain. Voiding unchanged.
NKDA.

Continued slow rise. Daughter and patient wish to keep the same approach. Continue observation; PSA in 6 months; return 1 year.

Urology

reports.text:
48-HOUR HOLTER MONITOR
Underlying rhythm sinus throughout. Occasional isolated premature ventricular complexes. No couplets. No ventricular tachycardia. No pauses. No atrial fibrillation.
reports.conclusion: Sinus rhythm with occasional isolated PVCs; no ventricular tachycardia.

documents.title: Cardiology Clinic Note
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
CARDIOLOGY CLINIC - FOLLOW-UP
3/10/2026

Seen with his daughter six weeks after admission for sustained VT, converted in the ED with IV amiodarone. No palpitations or lightheadedness since discharge. Taking metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily.

Testing since discharge:
- 48-hour Holter (2/16-2/18): sinus rhythm, occasional isolated PVCs, no VT.
- Pharmacologic (regadenoson) nuclear stress test (2/24): no ischemia, no infarct.
- Echo during admission: LVEF 55-60%, normal wall motion.

Meds: metformin, lisinopril 20, atorvastatin 40, metoprolol succinate 50, HCTZ 12.5.
Allergies: NKDA.

Impression: single episode of hemodynamically tolerated VT with preserved LV function and no ischemia on testing.

Plan:
- Continue metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily (we will prescribe).
- With normal LVEF, a defibrillator is not indicated at this time.
- Return in 6 months, sooner with palpitations, near-fainting or fainting.

Cardiology
